title: Lisinopril and Alcohol: Dizziness, Blood Pressure, and Kidney Risks
excerpt: Can you drink on lisinopril? How alcohol and this ACE inhibitor together lower blood pressure, why you get dizzy, the hangover painkiller trap, and when to call a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on lisinopril? Why the two cause dizziness, how drinking affects blood pressure and kidneys, plus safer hangover painkillers.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most people who take lisinopril can have an occasional drink, but the two together lower your blood pressure more than either one alone. That's why the most common problem is feeling dizzy or lightheaded, especially when you stand up quickly, get out of bed at night, or have been drinking in the heat. Heavy or regular drinking causes a second, slower problem: it pushes blood pressure back up and works against the medicine you're taking to bring it down. A third risk sits in the background for a big night out. Alcohol, vomiting, and diarrhea can dehydrate you, and dehydration combined with lisinopril (plus ibuprofen for the headache) can strain your kidneys.

**The quick rules:** Keep taking lisinopril as prescribed; don't skip a dose because you plan to drink. Keep it to light drinking, eat first, and alternate with water. Stand up slowly, sit down if the room spins, and be careful on stairs and getting up at night. Avoid ibuprofen and naproxen for a hangover unless your doctor has said they're fine for you. Ask your doctor or pharmacist what's a reasonable amount for you, because the answer depends on why you're on lisinopril and what else you take.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how lisinopril and alcohol interact in general terms. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on lisinopril if** you take it for heart failure, after a heart attack, or for kidney disease; you also take a water pill (such as hydrochlorothiazide, often combined with lisinopril in one tablet) or other blood pressure drugs; you've had fainting spells or falls; you have diabetes; or you've been told to watch your potassium. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room** if you faint, have chest pain, or notice swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing.

## How Lisinopril and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Lisinopril belongs to a group of blood pressure medicines called **ACE inhibitors**. Your body makes a hormone called angiotensin II that tightens blood vessels and tells the kidneys to hold on to salt and water. Lisinopril blocks the enzyme (ACE) that makes this hormone. With less of it around, blood vessels relax and your body holds less fluid, so blood pressure comes down. Doctors prescribe it for high blood pressure, heart failure, after a heart attack, and to protect the kidneys in people with diabetes.

Alcohol affects the same system from several directions at once:

1. **It relaxes blood vessels in the short term.** In the hours after drinking, alcohol widens blood vessels, which is why your face can feel warm and flushed. For many people, blood pressure dips a little in that window. Lisinopril is already keeping your vessels relaxed, so the two effects add up.
2. **It makes you lose fluid.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to save water, so you urinate more. A night of drinking, sweating on a dance floor, or vomiting the next morning can leave you noticeably low on fluid. Less fluid in your blood vessels means lower blood pressure, and lisinopril limits one of the ways your body would normally push back.
3. **It raises blood pressure over time.** Regular heavy drinking does the opposite of the short-term dip. Across many studies, drinking more than about two drinks a day is linked to higher blood pressure, and blood pressure often rises the day after a heavy session as the body rebounds. Cutting back is one of the lifestyle changes the American Heart Association recommends for people with high blood pressure.

So the interaction isn't a toxic chemical reaction like the one between [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). It's two things pulling on the same blood pressure controls. In the short term, they pull in the same direction, which can drop your pressure too far. Over the long term, alcohol pulls against the medicine.

### Why the lightheadedness happens when you stand up

When you go from lying or sitting to standing, gravity pulls blood toward your legs. Normally your body tightens blood vessels and speeds your heart within a second or two to keep blood flowing to your brain. Doctors call a failure of that reflex **orthostatic hypotension**, which simply means blood pressure that falls when you stand. Lisinopril blunts part of that tightening response, alcohol relaxes vessels further, and dehydration leaves less fluid to work with. Put together, you get the classic story: you feel fine sitting at the bar, then stand up and the room goes gray for a few seconds.

That brief grayness is usually harmless on its own. The danger is what happens if you fall. A lot of alcohol-related injuries in older adults on blood pressure medicines come from exactly this kind of fall, often at night on the way to the bathroom.

### The part most articles skip: the morning after

Most of the warnings about lisinopril and alcohol focus on the evening. In practice, the next morning can be just as risky, because that's when you're most dehydrated, may have been vomiting, and are likely to reach for a painkiller. If you take lisinopril in the morning, that dose lands while you're still low on fluid. That's the moment to drink water before your coffee, eat something, and get up slowly.

## Can You Drink Alcohol While Taking Lisinopril?

For most people, yes, in moderation. Lisinopril's prescribing information doesn't ban alcohol outright, but it does warn about low blood pressure in people who are low on fluid, and doctors and pharmacists generally advise limiting alcohol on any blood pressure medicine. Whether a particular amount is OK for you depends on a few things your doctor knows and a website doesn't:

- **Why you take it.** Someone on a low dose for mild high blood pressure has more room to spare than someone taking it for heart failure, where fluid balance and blood pressure are tightly managed.
- **What else you take.** Lisinopril is often combined with a water pill (lisinopril-hydrochlorothiazide, sold as Zestoretic and generics) or used alongside other blood pressure drugs such as amlodipine or metoprolol. Each one adds to the blood pressure drop. The hydrochlorothiazide label specifically notes that alcohol can make the drop in blood pressure on standing worse.
- **Your kidneys.** If your kidney function is already reduced, dehydration and lisinopril together matter more.
- **Your age.** Older adults are more prone to dizziness on standing and more likely to be hurt by a fall.

US dietary guidelines define moderate drinking as up to one drink a day for women and up to two for men, on days when people drink. That's a sensible ceiling for most people on lisinopril, and less is better for blood pressure. A "drink" is smaller than many people think: 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits. A large pour of wine or a craft beer at higher strength can easily count as two.

If you're newly started on lisinopril or your dose was just increased, it's worth holding off on drinking for the first week or two, or keeping it very light, until you know how the medicine affects you. Dizziness is most common early on.

## Lisinopril and Alcohol Side Effects: What to Watch For

These are the effects people most often notice when they drink on lisinopril:

- **Dizziness or lightheadedness**, especially when standing up. This is the main one.
- **Feeling faint or "graying out"** for a few seconds after getting up.
- **Unusual tiredness or weakness**, partly from lower blood pressure and partly from alcohol itself.
- **A worse-than-usual hangover headache and thirst**, mostly from dehydration.
- **Blurred vision or feeling unsteady** on your feet.

Less common but more serious effects need attention:

- **Fainting.** If you pass out, even briefly, tell your doctor. If you hit your head, have chest pain, or don't come round quickly, call 911.
- **Signs your kidneys are struggling.** Peeing much less than usual, swollen ankles, or feeling very unwell after a bout of vomiting or diarrhea while on lisinopril deserve a same-day call to a doctor.
- **Signs of high potassium.** Lisinopril can raise potassium. Muscle weakness, a slow or irregular heartbeat, or tingling are reasons to get checked.
- **Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat (angioedema).** This is a rare side effect of ACE inhibitors that can happen at any time, even after years on the drug. Alcohol isn't known to cause it, but don't write off sudden swelling as "just a puffy face from drinking." Puffy eyes and a slightly swollen face after a night out are common and mild (see our guide to [alcohol face bloating](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating)). Swelling of the lips or tongue, or any trouble breathing or swallowing, is an emergency. Call 911.

## Does Alcohol Raise Blood Pressure on Lisinopril?

In the short term, usually not; it more often lowers it for several hours. Over days and weeks, regular drinking does raise it, and lisinopril doesn't fully cancel that out.

The pattern looks like this. In the evening, while you're drinking and shortly after, blood pressure tends to dip. The following day, especially after several drinks, it can climb above your usual level as the effect wears off. If you drink heavily most days, the overall level creeps up. Research reviews have found that when heavy drinkers cut back, their blood pressure falls, and the drop is larger the more they were drinking to begin with.

This matters for a practical reason. If your home readings or clinic readings are high, your doctor may raise your lisinopril dose or add another drug. If the real driver is regular drinking, more medicine treats the number but not the cause, and it makes the evening dip after drinking deeper. Being honest with your doctor about how much you drink helps them get the dose right. Our guide on [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) covers this in more detail.

## Does Alcohol Make Lisinopril Stop Working?

Not directly. Alcohol doesn't block lisinopril or change how your body clears it. Lisinopril isn't broken down by the liver the way many drugs are; it leaves the body mostly unchanged through the kidneys. So the liver-enzyme interactions you read about with some other medicines don't apply here.

What alcohol does is work against the goal of the treatment. Regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure, adds calories, disrupts sleep, and can make it easier to forget doses. All of that can make your blood pressure harder to control even though the medicine itself is working as designed.

## How Long After Taking Lisinopril Can I Drink?

There's no special waiting period. Lisinopril is taken once a day and builds up to a steady level in your body over several days, so its effect is fairly constant around the clock. Spacing your drink a few hours from your dose doesn't make a meaningful difference to the interaction.

What does help:

- **Don't skip or delay your dose** to "make room" for drinking. Skipping makes your blood pressure less stable, and you get no real safety benefit.
- **Don't double up** the next day if you forgot. Take the next dose at the usual time unless your pharmacist tells you otherwise.
- **If you take it at bedtime**, be extra careful about getting up at night after drinking. Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before standing.
- **If you vomit soon after your dose**, don't take another one. Call your pharmacist for advice.

## Lisinopril Hangover: Why the Morning After Can Feel Worse

People on lisinopril sometimes say their hangovers hit harder. There's a plausible reason. A big part of a hangover is dehydration and the body's response to it: thirst, headache, fatigue, and dizziness. Lisinopril limits one of the hormone systems your body uses to hold on to salt and water when you're low on fluid, so the dehydration side of a hangover can feel more pronounced, and the dizziness on standing more noticeable.

A gentler morning after looks like this:

1. **Rehydrate before anything else.** Water is fine. A standard oral rehydration solution or a modest electrolyte drink is also fine for most people.
2. **Be careful with high-potassium products.** Lisinopril can raise potassium. A normal diet and an ordinary electrolyte drink are fine for most people, but if your doctor has told you to watch your potassium, or you have kidney disease, avoid potassium-based salt substitutes and check labels before drinking large amounts of high-potassium products. Ask your pharmacist if you're unsure. Our comparison of [electrolyte drinks for a hangover](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) lists what's in the popular ones.
3. **Eat something.** It steadies blood sugar and settles your stomach.
4. **Get up slowly.** Sit for a moment, then stand, then wait before walking.
5. **Choose your painkiller carefully** (see the next section).
6. **Skip "hair of the dog."** More alcohol just restarts the cycle and deepens the dehydration.

If you can't keep fluids down, have been vomiting for hours, or feel faint every time you stand, that's more than a normal hangover. Call a doctor or nurse line, or go to urgent care.

## The Painkiller Trap: Ibuprofen, Lisinopril, and Dehydration

This is the piece of the lisinopril and alcohol story that gets the least attention and causes some of the most real-world harm.

Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), and other anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) reduce blood flow into the kidneys' filters. On their own, at normal doses, in a well-hydrated person with healthy kidneys, that's usually not a problem. Lisinopril relaxes the blood vessel leading out of those filters. Combine the two with dehydration, and the pressure that drives filtering in the kidney can drop sharply. Pharmacists sometimes call the combination of an ACE inhibitor, a water pill, and an NSAID the **"triple whammy,"** because together they're a recognized cause of sudden kidney injury. A hangover adds a fourth factor: dehydration.

NSAIDs also tend to blunt the blood pressure-lowering effect of lisinopril if you use them regularly, and alcohol already irritates the stomach, which NSAIDs can make worse.

What that means in practice:

- **Avoid ibuprofen and naproxen for a hangover** unless your doctor has said they're fine for you. This matters most if you also take a water pill or have kidney disease.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** doesn't have this kidney effect and doesn't interact with lisinopril, but it has its own issue with alcohol, which is the liver. A single standard dose after the alcohol has cleared is usually reasonable for people who don't drink heavily. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the limits.
- **Low-dose aspirin** prescribed for your heart is a separate question; keep taking it as directed and ask your doctor about drinking. Our [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) and [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) guides cover those combinations.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Some people on lisinopril should check with their doctor before drinking at all, or keep it to the occasional single drink:

- **People with heart failure.** Fluid balance is the center of treatment, alcohol can weaken the heart muscle over time, and drops in blood pressure are harder to tolerate.
- **People with chronic kidney disease.** Dehydration plus an ACE inhibitor can push kidney function down, and potassium is more likely to run high.
- **People taking lisinopril with a water pill or other blood pressure drugs.** Each one adds to the drop on standing.
- **People with diabetes.** Lisinopril is often prescribed to protect the kidneys in diabetes. Alcohol can cause low blood sugar hours later, especially with insulin or sulfonylureas, and the shakiness and dizziness of low blood sugar can be mistaken for low blood pressure or a hangover. If you also take metformin, see our [metformin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/metformin-and-alcohol).
- **Older adults and anyone with a history of falls.** The consequences of a dizzy spell are bigger.
- **People who drink heavily most days.** Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal, which itself raises heart rate and blood pressure and can be dangerous. If that's you, talk to a doctor about cutting back safely rather than stopping on your own.

### "Sick day" guidance worth knowing

Some health services, including parts of the UK's NHS, give people on ACE inhibitors "sick day" advice: if you're having a dehydrating illness such as vomiting, diarrhea, or a fever with sweating, you may be told to pause certain medicines, including ACE inhibitors, until you're eating and drinking normally again, then restart. A bad stomach bug after drinking can fall into this category. **Don't stop lisinopril on your own based on this article**, because the right call depends on why you take it, especially with heart failure. Instead, ask your doctor or pharmacist at your next visit whether sick-day rules apply to you, so you know in advance.

## Practical Tips for a Night Out on Lisinopril

If you've checked with your doctor and you're going to drink, these habits make the evening and the next morning a lot easier:

- **Eat a proper meal first.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood, which softens the dip in blood pressure.
- **Set a limit before you go out** and count drinks honestly. One or two is a reasonable ceiling for most people on lisinopril.
- **Alternate every drink with a glass of water.** This is the single most useful habit for the dehydration side of the interaction.
- **Go easy in the heat**, at saunas and hot tubs, or with lots of dancing. Heat widens blood vessels too, and sweating adds to fluid loss.
- **Stand up slowly** after you've been sitting for a while, and hold a rail on stairs.
- **Don't drive.** Alcohol impairs driving on its own, and a dizzy spell at the wheel is a serious risk.
- **Watch the salt-free mixers and "lite" salt.** Potassium-based salt substitutes add potassium on top of lisinopril's effect.
- **Before bed, drink water and leave a glass by the bed.** Sit on the edge of the bed before standing if you get up in the night.
- **Take your next dose as usual**, after some water and food.

For more on drinking habits that reduce next-day misery, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## When to See a Doctor

Call your doctor or pharmacist soon if:

- You often feel dizzy or lightheaded after drinking, even after just one or two.
- Your home blood pressure readings are often high, and you drink most days.
- You've had a stomach bug or long bout of vomiting while on lisinopril and you're peeing much less than usual.
- You notice muscle weakness, an irregular heartbeat, or tingling (possible high potassium).
- You want to cut back on drinking and aren't sure how to do it safely.

Get emergency help (call 911) if:

- You faint and hurt yourself, have chest pain, or don't recover quickly.
- You have swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing.
- You're confused, extremely drowsy, or can't be woken easily after drinking.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people take supplements to make the morning after easier. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM changes how lisinopril works, and it has not been studied in people taking ACE inhibitors. It does nothing to prevent the blood pressure drop, the dehydration, or the kidney risk described above, so it's not a substitute for drinking less, drinking water, and avoiding NSAIDs.

If you'd like to try it, check with your pharmacist first, since supplements can interact with prescription medicines in ways that aren't well studied. Popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about combining it with common medicines.

## The Bottom Line

Lisinopril and alcohol both lower blood pressure in the short term, so drinking on lisinopril mainly risks dizziness, fainting, and falls, especially when you stand up, when you're dehydrated, and the morning after. Over the long term, regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure and works against the medicine. A big night with vomiting and ibuprofen on top adds a real risk to your kidneys. For most people, a drink or two with food, plenty of water, slow movements, and acetaminophen instead of ibuprofen keeps things safe. Keep taking your lisinopril as prescribed, be honest with your doctor about how much you drink, and ask what limit makes sense for you.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking lisinopril?**

For most people, light drinking is OK, but check with your doctor first. Alcohol and lisinopril both lower blood pressure, so together they can cause dizziness and lightheadedness, especially when you stand up. Keep it to one or two drinks with food and water. People with heart failure, kidney disease, or who also take a water pill should ask their doctor before drinking at all.

**What are the side effects of mixing lisinopril and alcohol?**

The most common are dizziness, lightheadedness on standing, tiredness, and a worse-feeling hangover from dehydration. Less often, the combination can cause fainting. If you're dehydrated from vomiting or diarrhea, it can also strain the kidneys, especially if you take ibuprofen or naproxen. Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat is a rare lisinopril side effect that needs emergency care.

**How long after taking lisinopril can I drink alcohol?**

There's no set waiting time. Lisinopril is taken once a day and stays at a fairly steady level in your body, so spacing a drink a few hours from your dose doesn't change much. Take your dose as usual, don't skip it to make room for drinking, keep the amount small, and stand up slowly afterward.

**Does alcohol raise blood pressure if you're on lisinopril?**

In the first few hours, alcohol usually lowers blood pressure a little, which adds to lisinopril's effect. Over the following day and with regular drinking, it tends to raise blood pressure. Drinking more than about two drinks a day on a regular basis is linked to higher blood pressure and can make it harder for lisinopril to keep your numbers in range.

**Can I take ibuprofen for a hangover if I'm on lisinopril?**

It's best to avoid it unless your doctor has said it's fine for you. Ibuprofen and naproxen reduce blood flow to the kidneys, and combined with lisinopril and the dehydration of a hangover, that can strain the kidneys, especially if you also take a water pill. Acetaminophen doesn't have this effect, but stick to one standard dose after the alcohol has cleared, because acetaminophen and alcohol carry a liver risk.

**Should I skip my lisinopril dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Skipping a dose makes your blood pressure less stable and doesn't make drinking safer. Take lisinopril at your usual time. If you vomit soon after a dose, don't take another; call your pharmacist. If you've had a dehydrating illness, ask your doctor whether you should pause it, rather than deciding on your own.

**Is it safe to drink electrolyte drinks on lisinopril?**

For most people, yes. Water and ordinary oral rehydration or electrolyte drinks are fine for a hangover. Lisinopril can raise potassium, so if your doctor has told you to watch your potassium or you have kidney disease, avoid potassium-based salt substitutes and check labels before drinking large amounts of high-potassium products. Ask your pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Does DHM interact with lisinopril?**

There is no good evidence either way. DHM hasn't been studied in people taking lisinopril or other ACE inhibitors, and it does not prevent the blood pressure drop or dehydration that come from mixing alcohol with lisinopril. If you want to try a DHM supplement, check with your pharmacist first and keep following the same drinking precautions.
